questions.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.solution:
For a uniform disc about the central perpendicular axis, $I = \mathbf{\tfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}}$.

Compare the standard results: a ring is $MR^{2}$ (all mass at the rim), a solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^{2}$, a hollow sphere $\tfrac{2}{3}MR^{2}$.

The pattern is that the further the mass sits from the axis, the larger the moment of inertia.

questions.q: A skater pulls her arms in while spinning. Her angular velocity:
questions.solution:
No external torque acts about the spin axis, so angular momentum $L = I\omega$ is conserved.

Pulling the arms in brings mass closer to the axis, **reducing** $I$. With $L$ fixed, $\omega$ must **increase**.

Her kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} = L^{2}/2I$ also rises — supplied by the muscular work of pulling the arms in against the outward pull.

$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, in that order.

It is a cross product, so the magnitude is $rF\sin\theta$ — a force applied along the line to the axis ($\theta = 0$) gives no torque, which is why you push a door at the edge and perpendicular to it.

$\vec{F}\times\vec{r}$ is the same vector reversed, so the order matters.

questions.q: A solid sphere, a disc and a ring of the same mass and radius roll down the same incline from rest. Which reaches the bottom first?
questions.solution:
For rolling without slipping, $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^{2}/R^{2}}$, where $I = mk^{2}$.

$k^{2}/R^{2}$ is $\tfrac{2}{5}$ for the sphere, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ for the disc, $1$ for the ring.

The **smallest** ratio gives the largest acceleration, so the **solid sphere** wins. Mass and radius do not appear — only the shape does.

questions.q: An isolated system explodes into fragments. The centre of mass of the system:
questions.solution:
Internal forces cannot change the total momentum of a system. The explosion supplies only internal forces, so

$\vec{v}_{\text{cm}}$ is **unchanged**.

A shell bursting in flight has fragments flying everywhere, yet their centre of mass carries on along the original parabola.

questions.q: The parallel axis theorem states that:
questions.solution:
$I = I_{cm} + Md^{2}$, where $d$ is the distance between the two parallel axes and $I_{cm}$ is about the one through the centre of mass.

The added term is always positive, so **the moment of inertia is least about an axis through the centre of mass** — a useful check on any answer.

questions.q: The rotational analogue of Newton's second law is:
questions.solution:
Replacing force by torque, mass by moment of inertia and linear acceleration by angular acceleration gives $\mathbf{\tau = I\alpha}$.

The other options are real equations but different ones: $L = I\omega$ is angular momentum (the analogue of $p = mv$) and $W = \tau\theta$ is rotational work.

questions.q: For a body rolling without slipping, the fraction of its total kinetic energy that is rotational is:
questions.solution:
Total $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$, with $I = mk^{2}$ and $\omega = v/R$:

$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}\right)$

The rotational part is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\dfrac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}$, so the fraction is $\mathbf{\dfrac{k^{2}/R^{2}}{1 + k^{2}/R^{2}}}$.

For a ring that is $\tfrac{1}{2}$; for a solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{7}$.

$\dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}}$, so $\vec{L}$ is constant precisely when the **net external torque is zero**.

That is weaker than requiring zero force: a planet orbiting the Sun feels a large force but no torque about the Sun, because the force is along $\vec{r}$ — which is exactly why Kepler's second law holds.

questions.q: Find the moment of inertia, in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$, of a ring of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ and radius $0.5\ \text{m}$ about its central perpendicular axis.
questions.solution:
For a ring, all the mass is at distance $R$ from the axis, so

$I = MR^{2} = 2 \times (0.5)^{2} = 2 \times 0.25 = \mathbf{0.5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}}$.

questions.q: A force of $10\ \text{N}$ acts perpendicular to a rod at $0.4\ \text{m}$ from the pivot. Find the torque, in $\mathrm{N\,m}$.
A disc spinning at $\omega$ has its moment of inertia halved with no external torque. By what factor does its angular velocity change?
questions.solution:
Angular momentum is conserved:

$I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$

$I\omega = \left(\tfrac{I}{2}\right)\omega_2$

$\omega_2 = \mathbf{2\omega}$ — the angular velocity **doubles**.

questions.q: A torque of $6\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ acts on a body of moment of inertia $3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$. Find the angular acceleration, in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$.
Masses of $2\ \text{kg}$ and $3\ \text{kg}$ sit at $x = 0$ and $x = 5\ \text{m}$. Find the position of the centre of mass, in metres from the origin.
questions.solution:
$x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

$= \dfrac{2(0) + 3(5)}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{15}{5} = \mathbf{3\ \text{m}}$.

As expected, it lies nearer the heavier mass.

questions.q: A body of mass $m$, radius $R$ and moment of inertia $I = mk^{2}$ rolls without slipping down an incline of angle $\theta$. Derive its linear acceleration, and hence compare a solid sphere with a ring.
questions.solution:
**Forces.** Along the incline, the component of weight $mg\sin\theta$ drives the body down and friction $f$ acts **up** the slope — it is friction that supplies the torque making the body rotate rather than slide.

Translation: $mg\sin\theta - f = ma$ ... (1)

**Rotation** about the centre of mass. Only friction has a moment arm about that axis:

$fR = I\alpha = mk^{2}\alpha$ ... (2)

**The rolling condition.** Rolling without slipping means the contact point is instantaneously at rest, which gives $v = \omega R$ and hence

$a = \alpha R \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{a}{R}$ ... (3)

**Solving.** Substituting (3) into (2):

$f = \dfrac{mk^{2}a}{R^{2}}$

Putting that into (1):

$mg\sin\theta - \dfrac{mk^{2}a}{R^{2}} = ma$

$g\sin\theta = a\left(1 + \dfrac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}\right)$

$\boxed{a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^{2}/R^{2}}}$

**What it says.** The mass and the radius have both cancelled. Only the *shape*, through $k^{2}/R^{2}$, decides how fast a body rolls down — which is not at all obvious and is the whole point of the result.

**Comparison.**

Solid sphere: $k^{2}/R^{2} = \tfrac{2}{5}$, so $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1.4} \approx 0.71\,g\sin\theta$.

Ring: $k^{2}/R^{2} = 1$, so $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{2} = 0.5\,g\sin\theta$.

The sphere accelerates about $1.4$ times as fast and reaches the bottom first. Physically, the ring carries all its mass at the rim, so a larger share of the released potential energy has to go into rotation and less is left for translation.
